ai.literal: Even though revolving, behind the plough is the world; therefore, even with toil, agriculture indeed is foremost.
ai.translation: Though the world wanders through many diverse occupations, it must ultimately follow the plough; therefore, despite the hard toil it demands, agriculture is the foremost occupation.
ai.modern: உலகம் பல தொழில்களில் சுழன்று திரிந்தாலும் ஏரின் பின்னாலேயே செல்ல வேண்டியிருக்கிறது; அதனால், எவ்வளவு துன்பப்பட்டு உழைத்தாலும் உழவுத் தொழிலே முதன்மையானது ஆகும்.
ai.explanation: This couplet establishes the supreme importance of agriculture over all other professions. The poet notes that although people wander and engage in various trades to make a living, the entire world ultimately depends on the food produced by the plough. The word 'suḻaṉṟum' suggests the restless wandering of humanity in search of livelihoods, which always leads back to the soil. Therefore, despite the physical hardship and intense labor implied by 'uḻantum', farming remains the most vital and noble pursuit.

words.gloss: to the people of the world

ai.literal: Those who plough are the linchpin to the people of the world, supporting all those who, not performing that, rise.
ai.translation: Those who plough are the linchpin of the world, for they support all others who, unable to plough, rise to pursue other callings.
ai.modern: உழவு செய்பவர்கள் உலகத்தாருக்கு அச்சாணி போன்றவர்கள்; ஏனென்றால், உழவு செய்யாமல் மற்ற தொழில்களைச் செய்யப் புறப்படுபவர்கள் எல்லாரையும் தாங்கி நிற்பது அவர்களே.
ai.explanation: This couplet highlights the central importance of agriculture to society by comparing farmers to a linchpin (ஆணி) of a chariot. Just as a small linchpin holds the entire wheel and chariot together, the farmers sustain the entire world. The phrase 'அஃது ஆற்றாது எழுவாரை' refers to those who do not or cannot perform the work of ploughing and instead rise to pursue other professions. By producing food, farmers bear the burden of supporting all these other professionals, making agriculture the foundational support of all human activity.

ai.literal: Those who live by ploughing and eating are indeed those who live; all others, having worshipped and eaten, are those who go behind.
ai.translation: Only those who live by tilling the soil and eating their own food truly live; all others must bow down to them, eat, and follow in their wake.
ai.modern: உழுது பயிர் செய்து அதனால் வரும் உணவை உண்டு வாழ்பவர்களே உண்மையாக வாழ்பவர்கள் ஆவர்; மற்றவர்கள் அனைவரும் பிறரைத் தொழுது, அவர்கள் தரும் உணவை உண்டு, அவர்களுக்குப் பின்னே செல்பவர்கள் ஆவர்.
ai.explanation: This couplet highlights the supreme importance and independence of agriculture. The poet asserts that farmers, who till the soil and feed themselves, are the only ones who lead a truly independent and dignified life. All other people, regardless of their status, depend on the food produced by farmers. Consequently, they must bow to the producers of food, receive sustenance from them, and follow them as dependents.

ai.literal: Even the shade of many umbrellas, under their own umbrella, they will see—those who have the shade of possessing ears of grain.
ai.translation: Those who live under the shade of the grain-yielding plough will see the sovereign umbrellas of many other kings brought under the shade of their own ruler's umbrella.
ai.modern: நெற்கதிர்களை உடைய உழவுத் தொழிலின் நிழலில் வாழ்பவர்கள், பல அரசர்களின் குடை நிழல்களையும் தங்களது அரசனுடைய குடை நிழலின் கீழ் வரக் காண்பார்கள்.
ai.explanation: This couplet highlights the supreme political and economic power that stems from agriculture. The umbrella (குடை) is a classical symbol of royal sovereignty and protection. The poet states that those who work under the 'shade of grain' (அலகுடை நீழலவர்), meaning the farmers, ultimately empower their own king to bring all other rulers under his dominion. Because every kingdom depends on food for survival, a nation with a thriving agricultural base naturally commands the allegiance and respect of other states.

ai.literal: They will not beg; to those who beg, they will give something without hiding, those whose nature is eating by working with their hands.
ai.translation: Those whose nature is to eat only by working with their own hands will never beg from others; instead, they will generously give to those who ask, without hiding what they have.
ai.modern: தன் கைகளால் உழைத்து உண்ணும் இயல்புடையவர்கள் யாரிடமும் இரந்து கேட்க மாட்டார்கள்; மாறாக, இரப்பவர்களுக்குத் தம்மிடம் உள்ளதை மறைக்காமல் கொடுப்பார்கள்.
ai.explanation: This couplet highlights the dignity and generosity of those who live by manual labor, specifically farmers. The phrase 'கைசெய்தூண் மாலை யவர்' refers to people whose character or habit ('மாலை') is to eat ('ஊண்') by working ('செய்து') with their own hands ('கை'). Because they are self-reliant, they will never beg ('இரவார்') from others. Instead, when others come to them seeking help, they will give ('ஈவர்') something ('ஒன்று') without concealing ('கரவாது') their resources. Through this, the poet emphasizes that honest labor not only preserves self-respect but also enables true charity.

ai.literal: If the ploughmen's hands are folded, there is no stability of existence even for those who say we have renounced all that is desired.
ai.translation: If the hands of ploughmen are folded in idleness, there is no stability of life even for those who claim to have renounced all worldly desires.
ai.modern: உழவர்களுடைய கைகள் வேலை செய்யாமல் முடங்கிப் போனால், 'நாங்கள் ஆசைகளைத் துறந்துவிட்டோம்' என்று கூறும் துறவிகளுக்கும் கூட இவ்வுலகில் வாழ வழியில்லாமல் போகும்.
ai.explanation: This couplet emphasizes that agriculture is the ultimate support for every member of society, including those who have withdrawn from worldly life. The phrase 'கைம்மடங்கின்' metaphorically describes farmers stopping their work, while 'விட்டேம் என்பார்' refers to ascetics who have renounced all desires. Even though these ascetics have given up material wants, they still require food to sustain their physical existence. Without the active labor of the ploughmen, even the most detached spiritual seekers cannot survive, proving that all human existence relies on the farmer.

ai.literal: If a todi of ploughed soil is dried to a quarter-measure, even a handful of manure without needing, abundantly it will yield.
ai.translation: If ploughed soil is dried so thoroughly that a measure of one todi shrinks to a quarter-measure, the land will yield abundantly even without a handful of manure.
ai.modern: உழுத மண்ணின் ஒரு பலம் எடையுள்ள புழுதி, காய்ந்து கால் பலம் எடையாகக் குறையும் அளவுக்குக் காய வைத்தால், ஒரு கைப்பிடி அளவு எருவும் தேவையில்லாமல் பயிர்கள் மிகச் சிறப்பாக விளையும்.
ai.explanation: This couplet highlights the supreme importance of thoroughly drying ploughed soil before sowing. The poet uses precise ancient weights: a 'toṭi' (equivalent to a 'palam') and a 'kaḥcu' (one-fourth of a 'toṭi'). If the wet, ploughed soil is left to dry in the sun so intensely that its moisture evaporates completely, reducing its weight to a quarter of its original wet weight, the soil becomes exceptionally fertile. Such well-dried soil becomes so rich in nutrients and aeration that the farmer does not even need to add a single handful of manure ('piṭittu eruvum vēṇṭātu') to get an abundant harvest ('cālap paṭum').

ai.literal: Even than ploughing, good indeed is applying manure; after weeding, even than watering, good is its protection.
ai.translation: Applying manure is better than mere ploughing; and once weeding is done, guarding the crop is even more important than watering it.
ai.modern: ஏர் பூட்டி உழுவதை விட எருவிடுவது நல்லது; களை எடுத்த பிறகு, நீர் பாய்ச்சுவதை விட பயிரைக் காவல் காப்பது நல்லது.
ai.explanation: This couplet outlines the practical hierarchy of agricultural tasks to ensure a bountiful harvest. The author explains that while ploughing ('ஏர்') is the fundamental first step, applying manure ('எரு விடுதல்') is far more beneficial to the soil's fertility. Similarly, once the weeds are cleared ('கட்ட பின்'), protecting the growing crop ('காப்பு') from external threats is even more critical than watering it ('நீர்'). The verse emphasizes that consistent care and vigilant protection are the ultimate keys to farming success.

ai.literal: Without going, if the owner remains, the land, feeling neglected, like a wife, will feign anger.
ai.translation: If the owner remains idle without visiting his field, the land, feeling neglected, will sulk and feign anger like a wife.
ai.modern: நிலத்தின் உரிமையாளன் நிலத்திற்குச் செல்லாமல் சோம்பேறியாக இருந்தால், அவனது நிலமானது தன்னை அவன் கைவிட்டுவிட்டதாக எண்ணி, அவனது மனைவி ஊடல் கொள்வது போலக் கோபித்துக் கொள்ளும்.
ai.explanation: This couplet uses a beautiful domestic metaphor to emphasize the necessity of constant personal attention in agriculture. The poet compares the land to a wife (illāḷ) who expects her husband's presence and care. If the owner (kiḻavaṉ) remains idle and fails to visit his fields (cellāṉ iruppiṉ), the land feels neglected (pulantu) and reacts with resentment (ūṭi viṭum), refusing to yield its bounty. Just as a neglected wife withdraws her affection, the neglected earth withdraws her fertility, showing that farming requires daily devotion and cannot be managed from afar.

ai.literal: If she sees those who sit idle, saying 'we have nothing' and being lazy, the good lady called Earth will laugh.
ai.translation: If the good lady called Earth sees those who sit idle, lazily complaining 'we have nothing,' she will laugh in mockery.
ai.modern: "எங்களிடம் ஏதும் இல்லை" என்று சோம்பேறியாக அமர்ந்திருப்பவர்களைக் கண்டால், பூமிதேவி என்னும் நல்லவள் பார்த்துச் சிரிப்பாள்.
ai.explanation: This couplet highlights the value of agricultural labor and the absurdity of complaining about poverty while refusing to work the land. The poet personifies the Earth as a 'good lady' (நல்லாள்) who is ready to yield wealth to those who toil. When people sit idle, lazily complaining that they have nothing, the Earth laughs at their foolishness because the source of abundance is right beneath their feet, waiting to be cultivated. The word 'அசைஇ' denotes being lazy or inactive, and 'நகும்' indicates her mocking laughter at their self-imposed poverty.
